big: Rebalancing means selling what rose and buying what fell, to get back to your target weights. It is simple on paper. Done by hand, every sale can leave a tax bill behind.

lines: I will just hold equity, debt and gold funds myself and rebalance once a year. Why pay for a multi-asset fund to do that?
You can. But watch what one year of rebalancing costs you, in rupees, before you decide.

h: A rally pushes the mix off target

caps: Start: ₹1 crore as 40% equity, 40% debt, 20% gold.
Equity rises 50%. The portfolio is now ₹1.2 crore, and equity is half of it.
To get back to 40%, sell ₹12 lakh of equity and put ₹8 lakh in debt and ₹4 lakh in gold.
Or add ₹30 lakh of new money to debt and gold. Same weights, no sale.
If you hold the three funds yourself, every sale is a tax event. Hold that thought.

alt: Two bars comparing tax and exit load of rebalancing by hand with rebalancing inside a fund
caps: The ₹12 lakh sold had cost ₹8 lakh. A gain of ₹4 lakh sits inside it.
Units held under a year: 20% short-term tax on ₹4 lakh is ₹80,000.
Add an exit load of 1%, assumed here: ₹12,000. That is ₹92,000, about 0.8% of the portfolio.
Inside a multi-asset fund the manager trades with no tax bill reaching you. You are taxed on redeeming.

h: Held for over a year instead?
intro: The same ₹12 lakh sale, but the units are more than 12 months old.
note: Assumes no other equity gains that year and ignores cess. Lower than ₹80,000, but still a bill every time you rebalance.

q: A ₹1 crore portfolio at 40% equity, 40% debt and 20% gold sees equity rise 50%, so it is worth ₹1.2 crore. How much equity must be sold to return to 40%?
opts: ₹20 lakh, which is the whole gain that equity has made since the start date
₹10 lakh, since equity moved ten points above its 40% target weight today
₹12 lakh: 40% of ₹1.2 crore is ₹48 lakh, and equity now stands at ₹60 lakh
₹24 lakh, since half of the equity holding must be sold to go back to target
why: Selling the whole gain would take equity below 40%, to ₹40 lakh, which is a third of the portfolio.
The ten points apply to a portfolio of ₹1.2 crore now, not ₹1 crore, and the target changes with size too.
Target equity is 0.4 times ₹1.2 crore, which is ₹48 lakh. Equity is at ₹60 lakh, so ₹12 lakh is sold.
Selling half would leave ₹30 lakh, a quarter of the portfolio. That overshoots the target by a lot.

q: The ₹12 lakh of equity sold had cost ₹8 lakh and was held under a year. Short-term equity gains are taxed at 20%. What is the tax, before cess?
opts: ₹80,000, since the gain is ₹4 lakh and 20% of that is ₹80,000
₹2,40,000, since 20% applies to the whole ₹12 lakh that was sold
₹50,000, since 12.5% applies to the gain of ₹4 lakh at the long-term rate
₹4,00,000, since the whole gain on the sale is paid out as tax in full
why: Tax applies to the gain only. The gain is ₹12 lakh minus ₹8 lakh, and 20% of ₹4 lakh is ₹80,000.
Tax is on the gain, not on the sale amount. Taxing ₹12 lakh would charge her on money she put in herself.
12.5% is the long-term rate. Units held under a year are short-term, so 20% applies.
The gain is the amount taxed, not the tax itself. The tax is a fraction of it.

q: A retired client holds three separate funds and the equity fund has drifted high. She asks how to restore her mix with the least tax. What should the adviser suggest first?
opts: Sell the extra equity at once, since drift is dangerous and the tax can be sorted out later
Direct fresh money and SIPs to the lagging assets, selling only if that falls short
Ignore the drift for ten years, because rebalancing never helps anyone in the end, ever
Switch the whole equity fund into the debt fund so that the mix is exactly right
why: Selling at once may trigger a short-term gain and an exit load. Cheaper routes exist before a sale.
New money moves the weights without a sale, so no gain is realised. It is the cheapest lever when money is flowing in.
Drift raises risk beyond what she signed up for. Leaving it for years is not a plan.
A switch is a sale plus a purchase, so it triggers the same tax. Moving everything also overshoots.

q: After gold's 2025 to 2026 rally, many multi-asset funds trimmed gold. Does a holder of such a fund owe tax on that trimming?
opts: Yes, on the share of the gold gain that falls to her units each time the fund trims
Yes, but only if she bought her units in the same financial year as the trimming
No, and she pays none even on redeeming, since gains inside a fund are never taxed
No. The fund trades within itself; the holder is taxed when units are redeemed
why: The trim is the fund's transaction. Nothing is passed to each holder as a taxable sale at that point.
When she bought is not the trigger. Her own redemption of units is the taxable event.
Redemption is taxed according to the fund's class. Nothing about internal trading removes that.
The fund's internal trades are not the investor's sale. Her tax arises on redemption, by the fund's tax class.

pts: Rebalancing sells what rose and buys what fell. By hand, a sale of ₹12 lakh with a ₹4 lakh gain can cost ₹80,000 short-term, plus any exit load.
Cheaper first: aim fresh money and SIPs at the lagging asset. Sell only when that cannot fix the drift.
Inside a multi-asset fund the manager rebalances without a tax event for you. You are taxed when you redeem.
